# INC-5521: Oversold stock and stuck holds during the September flash sale

Reported by the checkout team after the 2026-09-12 flash sale.

## What we saw

- The `sneaker-limited` drop had 250 units. We confirmed 263 orders, and 13
  customers had to be refunded.
- The stock dashboard showed `reserved` going negative for two SKUs after the
  sale, and it has not recovered.
- Some customers who retried checkout after a timeout had units held twice for
  one order; the second hold only disappeared when the reservation expired.
- One order was rejected because a bundle item was out of stock, but the other
  item in the bundle stayed held until we restarted the worker pool.
- Finance reports `sold` counts that are higher than the number of orders we
  shipped for a few SKUs.

## Context

Every checkout worker calls `InventoryService` concurrently. During the sale
we ran 40 workers. The nightly `expire()` job ran once during the sale.

The unit tests all pass, and none of this reproduces when we click through
checkout by hand.

A service-wide lock (INC-5490) stopped the overselling in staging but cut
checkout throughput by 90% and was rolled back the same day.

`committed` or `released`. Every checkout worker calls it concurrently.

```js
const { InventoryService, InsufficientStockError } = require('./src');

const inventory = new InventoryService(); // or { store, reservationTtlMs, now }
await inventory.addStock('sneaker-limited', 250);

try {
  await inventory.reserve('order-123', [{ sku: 'sneaker-limited', qty: 1 }]);
  await inventory.commit('order-123');   // or release('order-123')
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof InsufficientStockError) {
    // sold out: err.sku, err.requested, err.available
  }
}

await inventory.expire(); // nightly: releases reservations older than the TTL
```

`keys(prefix)`. `src/store.js` is an in-memory version with the latency
profile of the production Redis cluster.

| Symptom in ISSUE.md | Cause | Fix | Tests (`tests/incident.test.js`) |

| 263 orders confirmed for 250 units | Every counter update was a read-modify-write across two store round trips with nothing guarding it. A retry that arrived while the first attempt was in flight found no record and held the stock again. The record then covered one hold, so the second hold was never returned. | `reserve()` holds the order's lock for the whole call, so a retry waits for the attempt in flight and then returns its reservation. | `a retried checkout held units twice …` |

  take no lock.

  lock always comes before any SKU lock. That fixed order is why two bundles
  that list the same SKUs in different orders cannot deadlock.
- The lock table belongs to the store object, not the service. Several
  `InventoryService` instances built on one store (one per worker, say) lock
  against each other as well as against their own calls.

  grow with the number of SKUs or orders and nothing needs cleaning up. The
  service has no timers or connections, so there is no `close()`.

  locks, so the nightly job adds no more delay to a checkout call than one
  release would.

  has `get` and `set`. Each reserve holds the SKU's lock for three store
  round trips: read the counters, write them, write the order record.

  of its SKUs already holds the SKU locks that sort before it, so another
  call on one of those SKUs waits too. That call shares a SKU with the
  bundle, so this does not break the rule above. Locks are FIFO, so no call
  starves.

  transaction. If a write fails after the store actually applied it (for

```sh
npm test
```

| --- | --- |

| `tests/locks.test.js` | `KeyedLock`: mutual exclusion, parallelism, FIFO, deadlock freedom, cleanup |

content.text:
I found five causes behind the incident's symptoms and fixed them in `src/`. The full suite (68 tests) passes, and I ran it three times to check for flakiness.

## What caused each symptom

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 263 orders for 250 units | Every counter update read a value, changed it, and wrote it back with nothing guarding the gap. Concurrent reserves all read the same `reserved`, all passed the stock check, and the last write won. `commit` and `addStock` lost updates the same way. | A lock for each SKU and each order. |
| `reserved` negative | `release()` didn't check the order's status, so releasing a committed order took its units off `reserved` a second time. `expire()` called it on every old order, committed ones included. | `release()` now rejects a committed order with `OrderStateError`, as its doc comment says. `expire()` only releases orders still `reserved`, and re-checks that under the order's lock. |
| Retry held units twice | The retry check looks for the order record, which is only written at the end of `reserve()`. A retry that arrived mid-flight found nothing and held the stock again. | `reserve()` holds the order's lock for the whole call, so a retry waits for the first attempt and gets its reservation back. |
| Rejected bundle left an item held | Each item's hold was written before the next item was checked, and no order record existed to release it later. | Every item is checked before anything is written. If a store write fails, the items already written are put back. |
| `sold` higher than shipped | Overlapping commit retries each added to `sold`. A commit racing `expire()` could count units as sold and also mark the order released. | The order locks and status checks above. |

## How the locking works
- **No service-wide lock:** each SKU and each order has its own first-come-first-served lock, in the new file `src/locks.js`. Calls that share no SKU and no order never wait for each other.
- **No deadlocks:** a call takes the order's lock first, then its SKU locks in sorted order. Two bundles listing the same SKUs in opposite orders can't block each other.
